clinicalPearls: A pentose-phosphate-linked enzyme defect that impairs regeneration of reduced glutathione and predisposes to oxidant-induced haemolysis
The enzyme requires flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) as a cofactor, so acquired deficiency from dietary riboflavin lack can mimic or unmask the inherited defect
Haemolysis is typically episodic and oxidant-provoked rather than continuously present, with intervals of near-normal red-cell survival
Favism-like reactions and drug-induced haemolytic episodes have been described, overlapping clinically with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
Because the acquired riboflavin-responsive form exists, riboflavin status should be assessed and corrected before diagnosing a true genetic defect
Diagnosis rests on reduced enzyme activity that fails to normalise after FAD saturation in the genetic form, with GSR mutation testing
Management is supportive, centring on avoidance of oxidant drugs, correction of riboflavin deficiency and transfusion during severe crises
reference.pathophysiology: Glutathione reductase regenerates reduced glutathione from its oxidised form using NADPH supplied by the pentose phosphate pathway, sustaining the red cell's antioxidant defences. When enzyme activity is inadequate, reduced glutathione cannot be replenished quickly enough during oxidant stress, allowing oxidative damage to haemoglobin and the membrane and precipitating episodic haemolysis. The enzyme depends on FAD derived from dietary riboflavin, so nutritional riboflavin deficiency lowers activity and can produce an acquired form that resembles the rare inherited defect.
additionalDifferentials: Riboflavin (dietary) deficiency causing reduced enzyme activity
additionalInvestigations: Red-cell glutathione reductase activity assay, with and without FAD stimulation
Full blood count, reticulocyte count and blood film during episodes
Haemolysis screen with bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin
Direct antiglobulin test to exclude immune haemolysis
Molecular testing of the GSR gene where a genuine genetic defect is suspected
redFlags: Acute severe haemolysis following oxidant drug or food exposure
Failure to distinguish a correctable riboflavin deficiency from a genetic defect
Symptomatic anaemia during a crisis requiring transfusion
Aplastic crisis after parvovirus B19 infection
reference.prognosis: Between oxidant exposures many patients are asymptomatic with normal red-cell survival, and the acquired riboflavin-responsive form corrects with supplementation, giving an overall favourable prognosis when triggers are managed.
pitfalls: Diagnosing an inherited defect without first excluding and correcting riboflavin deficiency
Failing to stimulate the assay with FAD, missing the distinction between acquired and genetic forms
Not counselling avoidance of oxidant drugs and foods
Confusing episodic oxidant haemolysis with a chronic continuous process
